newsitem.title: USA: The roots behind one minority business success.
newsitem.headline: The roots behind one minority business success.

text.p: The Small Business Administration last week named Francisco Garcia its minority small business person of the year -- an award that surprised the Denver-based entrepreneur, who is used to toiling away in obscurity.
In Washington to receive the award, Garcia sat down and talked about what made his five-year old business a success and the price he has paid to achieve it.
"This caught me off guard," said Garcia, who was almost too busy running Integrated Information Technology Corp. to fill out the long questionnaire for nominees.
But he won a regional run-off and then the national award as well, though he said he didn't have anyone to take to the White House awards ceremony -- he has been too busy to have a social life.

Garcia's company specialises in telecommunications and information engineering, working on both government and private sector contracts. He started the business by himself in 1991 with $1,000. He currently has about 55 employees, and this year expects about $4.3 million in revenues.
"Next year, we'll be skyrocketing," he said.

Talking about his business, a few salient facts come to the foreground: he went into business for himself because he craved independence. He also had a good education and had befriended a successful businessman who became a mentor.
His company is also a member of the SBA's so-called 8 (a) programme that opens up federal contracts to business people who come from "socially and economically disadvanged" backgrounds.

Once in the programme, companies must "market" themselves to federal agencies, and if agencies want to do business with them, the SBA arranges the contract. "It gives you a shoe in the door but you have to make it happen," Garcia said.

The programme came under criticism this year, but Garcia is a staunch defender: "I still have to compete and market myself to get these contracts," He said. "It gives me an opportunity I would not have otherwise."
The programme was designed to raise the level of minority business participation in government contracts, which is now at 5.5 percent, as well as create jobs among minority-owned businesses.
Six thousand firms employing 154,000 now participate in the programme. They have been awarded $6.4 billion worth of contracts, according to the SBA.
Garcia is one of the program's success stories.

He was born in Mexico, raised in Texas and entered the Air Force shortly after graduating with a chemistry degree from the University of Texas. The Air Force then put him through school for an electrical engineering degree and he earned an MBA on his own.
"The Air Force was great to me," Garcia said, "but in the military you put your entire career in other people's hands." After seven years, he decided to get out.

His first job was at Modern Technologies Corp. in Dayton, Ohio. It was there that he introduced himself to the CEO, Rajesh Soin, and told him of his desire to start his own company. Garcia was then 28.
"We hit it off, we had a lot of similarities in the way we think," Garcia said. Soin pledged to help and once Garcia set up his business, his first subcontract was from his mentor.
At first he did everything himself, from the company accounts to its engineering and marketing. He made payroll by maxing out his credit cards, but steadily the business began to pick up steam.

Now he mostly concentrates on marketing -- a task that takes him away from home at least three weeks a month. One casualty was his family. He went through a divorce and now "my personal life is non-existent," he said.

While the business took all of his attention, it has also taken off. The 8 (a) government contracts have played a crucial role, but Garcia is also building up the commercial side with large communications companies.
He now has five regional offices around the country, in addition to his headquarters in Denver, and plans to open another office in the next three to six months in Atlanta or Washington, DC.

Garcia said the company has a strong services business because it stresses customer satisfaction. The next goal is to come up with a unique product, either equipment or software, that can differentiate the company and put it on the next plateau for growth.
